@tushushu thanks a lot for working on this! (and sorry for the slow reply on the original issue that I opened as well)

Reading through the PR comments here, I think there are two main outstanding issues:

**1\) What is the exact behaviour we want for the nullable dtypes (when involving NAs)?**

(re https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/38379#discussion_r541315635, https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/38379#issuecomment-751460846)

On current master, when having NA in the values, and not in the Series values, but not in the set values, you get False:

```python
In [3]: pd.Series([1, 2, pd.NA], dtype="Int64").isin([1])
Out[4]: 
0     True
1    False
2    False
dtype: bool
```

and True when the NA is present in the specified set:

```python
In [3]: pd.Series([1, 2, pd.NA], dtype="Int64").isin([1, pd.NA])
Out[4]: 
0     True
1    False
2     True
dtype: bool
```

This follows the current behaviour we have for NaNs with float dtype.

As @MarcoGorelli mentioned above, since pd.NA is unknown, it could also *propagate* (as it does for comparison operations). 
So the first example above could look like:

```python
>>> pd.Series([1, 2, pd.NA], dtype="Int64").isin([1])
0     True
1    False
2       NA
dtype: boolean
```

The question is then: what if NA is present in the values set to compare with? (the second case: `isin([1, pd.NA])`) Still propagate pd.NA, or then actually return True as we do now?

I think the question also boils a bit down to: do we see `s.isin([1, 2, ...])` as a shortcut for `(s ==1) & (s == 2) & ...` or as a shortcut for `[val in [1, 2, ...] for val in s]`? 
In tutorials, I typically explain it as a shortcut for multiple equality comparisons at once. But semantically, it could also perfectly makes sense that we say it should follow the behaviour of `in` (membership check with `__contains__`). And that's something that we recently discussed regarding NAs in https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/37867 (where we decided that `NA in pd.array([1, 2]]) -> False` and `NA in pd.array([1, 2, NA]) -> True` (so no propagation of NA).

It might be worth checking how other data science languages that might have similar functionality deal with this issue.

Final note here: the behaviour we choose should also be explicitly tested and documented for the nullable dtypes (which is not yet the case in this PR). And eg @jbrockmendel mentioned above the case of other missing value sentinels (np.nan, pd.NaT, None) in the values set, which we should also cover in the tests. 


**2\) Adding `isin` to the ExtensionArray interface**

To be clear, I am fully on board with adding an `isin` method. But, if we do that, it needs some more work than just the addition for nullable dtypes: we need to update the documentation for EA authors in base.py (*EDIT: which I see now is already mostly done!*), we need to add base extension tests (eg in `pandas/tests/extension/base/methods.py`) and ensure they pass for the different test extension arrays. 
And we also need to think about how external EA authors can implement this using the pandas provided functionalities Currently, the `isin` algorithm is only exposed as the Series method. Maybe this is enough, but for example for `take`, we exposed the base algorithm function to the `pd.api.extensions` namespace so external authors can make use of this. We should maybe do the same for `isin`?

BTW, for me it is fine to leave this more general topic for a separate PR, to limit the scope of this PR somewhat, and special case the masked arrays in this PR (although the tests might be overlapping anyway)

issue_context.title: ENH: implement fast isin() for nullable dtypes
issue_context.body:
Currently, you can get quite a slowdown:

```
In [41]: arr = np.random.randint(0, 10, 1_000_001)

In [42]: s = pd.Series(arr)

In [43]: %timeit s.isin([1, 2, 3, 20])
2.71 ms ± 175 µs per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 100 loops each)

In [44]: s = pd.Series(arr, dtype="Int64")

In [45]: %timeit s.isin([1, 2, 3, 20])
22.9 ms ± 96.7 µs per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 10 loops each)
```
comments: @jorisvandenbossche  Hi, I'm new here and would like to work on this issue.

@jorisvandenbossche  I found function `ensure_int64` could be the bottleneck, for it would cost about 20ms according to the example provided.

The whole debug path is:
-> pandas.Series.isin 
-> pandas.core.algorithms.isin 
-> pandas.core.algorithms._ensure_data 
-> pandas.core.dtypes.common.ensure_int64
-> pandas._libs.algos.ensure_int64

But I cannot find this function in algos.pyx or algos.pxd, could you please give some advices? Thanks very much.

@jorisvandenbossche 

We can see `Series's isin` method is calling `algorithms.isin` function.
https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/5cafae72a9c00da8e2f42f11c42b8fcb1639340a/pandas/core/series.py#L4633

And if we pass `s2._values._data` to `algorithms.isin` instead, the performance will be much better.
```Python
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
from pandas.core import algorithms

arr = np.random.randint(0, 10, 1_000_001)
s1 = pd.Series(arr)
s2 = pd.Series(arr, dtype="Int64")

%timeit algorithms.isin(s1._values, [1, 2, 3, 20])
1.87 ms ± 66.6 µs per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 100 loops each)

%timeit algorithms.isin(s2._values, [1, 2, 3, 20])
22.7 ms ± 851 µs per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 10 loops each)

%timeit algorithms.isin(s2._values._data, [1, 2, 3, 20])
1.86 ms ± 39.1 µs per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 1000 loops each)
```

So the solution could be:
```Python
from pandas.core.arrays.integer import IntegerArray

class Series:
    def isin(self, values) -> "Series":
        if isinstance(self._values, IntegerArray):
            result = algorithms.isin(self._values._data, values)
        else:
            result = algorithms.isin(self._values, values)
        return self._constructor(result, index=self.index).__finalize__( self, method="isin")
```

Looking forward to your reply.
